anomaly_def.Name: MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly : Accumulation of obsolete row versions and index entries outpaces background cleanup, inflating the version store and bloating data pages.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Engine-level settings for memory, checkpointing, worker throttles, and parallelism are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload demands, creating artificial bottlenecks.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The underlying storage subsystem reaches or nears its physical I/O bandwidth or IOPS limits, driving up read/write latency and queue depth.

When all three root causes strike together, the database experiences a feedback loop in which version churn rapidly enlarges tables and indexes, mis-calibrated parameters prevent aggressive vacuuming and amplify checkpoint bursts, and the swollen data plus write-heavy cleanup tasks saturate an already over-stressed storage layer. Observable symptoms converge: the version store and rollback segments grow without bound; autovacuum or purge workers stay perpetually active yet make little progress; checkpoint and log-flush waits spike even while CPU cores are idle; device-level latency soars, causing statement execution times and replication lag to lengthen; query plans degrade because optimizer statistics lag behind the bloated heap; and monitoring shows conflicting signals of low CPU but high wait ratios on buffer-I/O, log write, and vacuum-related events.

Causally, heavy UPDATE/DELETE workloads generate large numbers of dead tuples (MVCC anomaly). Because memory, autovacuum cost limits, and checkpoint intervals are misconfigured (configuration anomaly), the engine cannot reclaim space promptly and instead accumulates ever-larger dirty pages and WAL. The enlarged working set and prolonged checkpoints push sustained random and sequential I/O beyond what the disk subsystem can deliver (storage throughput anomaly). Elevated I/O latency further slows cleanup workers, lengthening the visibility horizon and accelerating version buildup. This vicious cycle intensifies page bloat, inflates WAL, and keeps the system trapped in a deteriorating state where each anomaly reinforces the others, ultimately threatening transaction-ID wraparound or instance unavailability.

entry.official_description: Max tablespace id is too high, %lu
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
